proof_nl: Fix an arbitrary real number x, and let m = floor(x). By the defining property of the floor function, m is an integer, m <= x, and m is the greatest integer with this property. Suppose, for contradiction, that x >= m + 1. Then m + 1 is an integer and also m + 1 <= x. But this contradicts the maximality of m, since m + 1 > m is a larger integer that still does not exceed x. Therefore the assumption is impossible, so x < m + 1. Substituting m = floor(x), we obtain x < floor(x) + 1. Since x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.
solver_summary: Let m = floor(x). If x were at least m+1, then m+1 would be a larger integer still <= x, contradicting the maximality of floor(x). Hence x < floor(x)+1 for all real x.
vetter_reason: The proof correctly applies the defining maximality property of floor(x): if m = floor(x), then m <= x and no larger integer can still be <= x. Assuming x >= m + 1 yields a contradiction, so x < m + 1, hence x < floor(x) + 1. The argument is complete and matches the lemma statement without semantic drift.
